summary: Learners aged 10–11 read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, and compare with >, =, < based on place-value meaning. The central hurdle is the 'longer-is-larger' error (judging 0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits). Guidance centres on place-value alignment, equalising with trailing zeros, naming decimals by their place ('sixty-two thousandths') to keep place meaning audible, and building expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers.
misconceptions: 'Longer decimal is larger' (0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits)
'Shorter decimal is larger' (over-correcting to 'fewer digits = closer to whole')
Reading 0.062 as 'point zero sixty-two' and losing the thousandths meaning
Treating the decimal part as a whole number after the point (comparing 372 vs 38)
Misplacing digits in expanded form — attaching 1/10 to the hundredths digit

activities.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart
steps: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
activities.insight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).

activities.title: Write spoken decimals keeping placeholder zeros
steps: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names: 'five and sixty-two thousandths' rather than 'five point zero six two'.
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as a numeral, anchoring the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third decimal place.
Fill the places: 062 occupies tenths–hundredths–thousandths, giving 5.062.
Explain where the placeholder 0 goes and why it cannot be dropped.
Translate in both directions: given 5.062, say the words; given the words, write the numeral.
activities.insight: Naming a decimal by its place ('thousandths') tells you which column the last digit must occupy; a placeholder zero may be needed so the digits land in the correct places. 5.062 ≠ 5.62.

activities.title: Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers
steps: Tap or point to each digit of a number such as 347.392 and name its place and value.
Write the expanded form binding each digit to its place: 3×100 + 4×10 + 7×1 + 3×(1/10) + 9×(1/100) + 2×(1/1000).
Say what each digit is worth, e.g. 'the 9 is worth 9 hundredths, 9×(1/100)'.
Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the decimal point: each place is one tenth of the place to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
Check a tricky case: the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10, NOT by 10 or 1.
activities.insight: Expanded form makes each digit's value explicit. Decimal places continue the base-ten pattern to the right with unit-fraction multipliers (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000), one tenth of the place to the left.

activities.title: Argue and justify a comparison (discussion)
steps: Respond to a prompt such as 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38, and prove it?'
Make a claim and justify it by aligning place values, not by counting digits.
Defend the claim against the 'longer-is-larger' bait by padding to 0.380 and comparing the hundredths.
Put the comparison into a sentence: '0.38 is bigger because they are equal in the tenths but 8 hundredths beats 7 hundredths.'
activities.insight: Being able to explain a comparison in words — citing the first differing place — demonstrates place-value understanding rather than rule-following.

activities.title: Check and order several decimals
steps: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and choose >, = or <, rejecting any answer based purely on digit count.
Complete 'five and sixty-two thousandths = ___' with the correct numeral (5.062).
Order four decimals of unequal length (e.g. 0.3, 0.29, 0.305, 0.31) by padding to equal length and comparing left-to-right, giving 0.29 < 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.31.
Explain each placement rather than only giving the final order.
activities.insight: Reading, writing and comparing decimals can be verified across numeral and word forms and by ordering, including deliberately mixed-length cases that expose the 'longer-is-larger' trap.

checkQuestion: Watch across forms. 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38? Line them up to decide. Write “five and sixty-two thousandths” as a decimal. Then write 347.392 in expanded form.' Watch the comparison reasoning and the placeholder zero in the thousandths write.
